#926. 'I can't believe he is one of us' - inside Salah's life in Trabzon

Mohamed Salah has scored 10 goals in 15 games for Turkish club Trabzonspor

Back in August, when Mohamed Salah landed in Istanbul after flying in from his holiday in Mykonos, he wore Trabzonspor's burgundy and blue home strip as he stepped out of the plane to be greeted by thousands of fans.

That kit sold out almost instantly. Later that day, as Salah headed to Trabzon in north-east Turkey to complete the formalities of one of the most unexpected transfers after the expiry of his Liverpool contract, he asked one of his entourage what he should wear.

"The same kit," came the response, but Trabzonspor president Ertugrul Dogan advised Salah to wear the black away kit instead. Of course, that sold out too.

From the outset of the 34-year-old's arrival to this historic port city on the Black Sea, that sense of adulation has only grown.

"I went to the airport to see him in Istanbul and it was surreal," says Nisa Dumangoz. "I still can't believe that he is one of us."

Go for a stroll through Trabzon on matchday and it is Salah's face which adorns everything. Even the walls inside the fishmongers have pictures of him.

At the club shop in town, one of the staff jokes that the ground floor is for the Egyptian and the upper floor is for everything else.

Outside the stadium, there are scarves, magnets, keyrings, lighters with his face on and Egyptian Nemes headdresses in Trabzonspor colours. Season ticket sales rocketed after his arrival.

"Walking around Trabzon, it feels as though nine out of every 10 fans wearing a shirt have Salah's name on the back. The 10th has their own," says Turkish football journalist Hasan Tuncel.

The club have surpassed their merchandise revenue from last year in three months since Salah's arrival, while the local airport is only getting busier.

Liverpool was difficult to reach for many supporters across the Arab world and tickets were often hard to source. Trabzon is far more accessible, with new flights introduced from Cairo, Dubai and Riyadh since Salah's arrival.

On our flight from Istanbul, we meet an Egyptian family of 10 coming from Cairo for Trabzonspor's Uefa Conference League game against Freiburg.

"He is our ambassador and our Egyptian King, and with how many people want to come to Turkey now, he is their ambassador too," says Mahmoud.

At the game, there is a group of Egyptian celebrities and influencers. A quick check of their social media shows their combined Instagram following of about five million. Trabzonspor have three million. Salah has 68 million.

Salah recently went for a hike and posed for a picture on a rock in the Trabzon highlands. That rock has been renamed Salahtasi (Salah's Rock) and is now a tourist destination.

The commercial element of his signing has more than been justified but crucially, on the pitch, Salah is driving Trabzonspor's push for the Turkish Super Lig title and he has hit the ground running with 10 goals and five assists in all competitions.

Trabzonspor trail leaders Galatasaray by three points, having won seven of their first 10 games, including victories against the table-toppers and Besiktas.

For context, the Istanbul 'big three' of Galatasaray (26), Fenerbahce (19) and Besiktas (16) have won the league on 61 occasions combined, compared with Trabzonspor's seven titles.

"In Turkey, he is the biggest football star after Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo," says Kerim Tonyali, who is part of Gurbetci Gencler, a Trabzonspor supporters' group.

And given Salah's status as an icon, Trabzonspor are quickly becoming the second club for many in Turkey and the wider Muslim world.

Salah's face is a common sight wherever you go in Trabzon

Trabzon may be more than 2,000 miles from Liverpool but there are similarities, particularly when it comes to the sense of identity and pride associated with originating from here.

"Everywhere is Trabzon for us," is the local mantra and aligns with the sense of unity within this city that has a population of about 800,000 and is only the 30th-biggest in Turkey.

For Salah, the financials were important and he is earning about Â£14.6m per year as well as 20% of official merchandise sold with his name on, but one of the key aspects of coming here was the ability to focus entirely on his football.

Besiktas was considered as an option after the 2026 World Cup but, after multiple calls with Trabzonspor, Salah felt they were the ideal fit and offered a life away from the hustle and bustle of Istanbul.

He has his own security detail and is living in the nearby town of Yomra, where he now has a street named after him. He also employs a private chef and, unsurprisingly, continues to set standards in the gym and on the training ground.

By all accounts, Salah is thriving. He is a fan of Turkish coffee and is often spotted leaving the ground with Ayran - a traditional yogurt drink - but as much as he wants to explore the city, he knows of the difficulties given his reputation.

"Everyone wants to work with a star like Mohamed Salah," said Trabzonspor's Paul Onuachu, formerly of Southampton. "He adds so much and helps all of us and he contributes positively. I am grateful for him. It's a blessing to play with him."

Watching Salah in the flesh in a Conference League game against Freiburg, his pace has gone down a notch compared with his peak but the touch, quick feet and sheer quality is still there. And so is that knack of getting in goalscoring positions, even if his defensive duties - which were such a source of debate last season at Liverpool - are limited.

Salah believes he still has plenty to give for club and country, with aspirations to play in both the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations and 2030 World Cup, which will be partly held in North Africa.

No decision has been made about how long he will stay in Turkey, but there is growing belief among sources in the Middle East that he will move to Saudi Arabia when his two-year Trabzonspor deal expires in 2028. By then, he will be 36.

Salah signed a two-year deal with Trabzonspor in the summer of 2026

On initial thoughts, it is easy to question how and why Salah ended up here.

When he delivered that infamous mixed-zone interview at Leeds' Elland Road less than a year ago and the wheels of his departure from Liverpool were set in motion, surely no-one would have imagined his next destination would be this Turkish outpost near the Georgian border.

"I remember looking at him when we landed in Trabzon and seeing the crowds outside and how emotional it was," says Anil Dincer, one of the lawyers involved in Salah's move to Turkey.

"We already have Salah and Fabinho. So now we are waiting for [Virgil] Van Dijk," adds Serhat Sumer, a Trabzonspor fan.

Salah, of course, delivered so much joy to Liverpool and the intention here is the same. This is no drift towards retirement, but a player determined to prove he still belongs at the highest level and that football still has meaning beyond trophies and money.

Asked by BBC Sport if he had a message for Liverpool fans, Salah simply said "hello" and smiled. Given how rarely he spoke in the mixed zone during his time at Anfield, it is not in his nature to talk regularly on record.

Last season was Salah's least prolific at Anfield, but given Liverpool's struggles in front of goal in the Premier League, it is hard to argue they have replaced one of their greatest ever players.

Perhaps a time will come when the likes of Salah, Arne Slot and Richard Hughes will reveal more about the chain of events that led to the forward agreeing to terminate his contract a year early. As it is, none of them are at the club and that chapter is firmly closed.

Salah's influence that once helped shape the Premier League is now being felt on the shores of the Black Sea. He is Trabzonspor's force of nature. And the team known as the Black Sea Storm are rising and on the hunt for silverware with their Egyptian King.

A rock in the Trabzon highlands became a tourist destination after Salah's visit

#925. What can you read into Premier League table after 10 games?

Only four teams have taken more points than Arsenal's 27 after 10 games

We are now more than a quarter of the way through the Premier League season, with each team having played 10 games.

History suggests the answer is quite a lot.

Last season, for instance, the top two - and two of the eventual bottom three - were in the exact spots at this stage that they in finished six months later.

How the Premier League table looks after 10 games

Arsenal are top of the table on 27 points - which is higher than the average number of points (23) champions have after 10 games.

In fact, only four teams have taken more points from their first 10 fixtures than the Gunners, and all four have gone on to win the league.

One small quirk that means Arenal fans should not start making plans for a parade just yet is that the only two previous sides to post exactly 27 points at this point of the campaign both failed to win the title - including the Gunners in 2022-23.

In 15 of the 34 Premier League seasons to date, the team top at this stage have gone on to win the title, so less than half the time.

While on 16 previous occasions, teams on 22 points, the tally of second-placed Brighton, or fewer after 10 games won the title, so there is still hope for the Seagulls.

However, the less good news for Fabian Hurzeler's side is that, bizarrely, the team in second after 10 games have won the title in just one of the past 18 seasons - that was Manchester City in 2022-23.

The fewest points any side has had at this stage and gone on to win the league is 18 - so City, on 21, and Liverpool, on 18, could still have a say.

Arsenal lead Brighton by five points, one fewer than the most points a team have ever come from behind at this stage to win a title.

Manchester United in 2002-03 and Manchester City in 2013-14 are the two to do that.

But Mikel Arteta and co can take comfort knowing the leaders at this stage have gone on to win the title in the past two seasons - after failing to do so in the previous four years.

Another 1-0 for relentless Arsenal - but did Odegaard spare VAR blushes?

Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top

Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit

Crystal Palace are propping up the table having lost their past four league matches, but the stats suggest their position is far from terminal.

In total, 14 teams have stayed up having been bottom of the table at this point in the season - most recently Wolves in 2024-25.

Moreover, the fewest points a team has had after 10 games and stayed up at the end of the season is three.

That same Wolves team are the most recent of the four teams to have achieved that feat.

Sunderland, who climbed off the foot of the table with victory over Chelsea, had just four points at this stage in 2013-14 but still ended up finishing 14th.

Palace can also count themselves a little unfortunate to have amassed seven points and find themselves in 20th.

Only Bolton in 2002-03 have had more points (eight) after 10 games and been bottom - and that was in a situation when a number of other sides had played 11 matches.

Overall, 88 teams have previously had seven or fewer points after 10 Premier League games and 37 managed to stay up.

There is good news for Ipswich and Hull in that every promoted side since 2015-16 to take 11 points or more from their first 10 games - and there have been 14 of them - has survived.

The most recent promoted side to make as bright a start and go down were Cardiff in 2013-14, who were 12th with 12 points but finished bottom on 30 points.

The outlook is a little bleaker for Coventry.

Only two promoted sides in the past 11 seasons have taken fewer than 11 points and survived - Bournemouth in 2015-16 (eight) and Nottingham Forest in 2022-23 (five).

Frank Lampard's men are also the seventh promoted side to take exactly nine points from their first 10 games - two of the previous six survived (Wolves in 2009-10 and Leicester in 2014-15).

Lampard feels hair pull should have led to Coventry penalty

A long way to go then, still plenty of time for things to change. But how much do things really change from this point?

Well, not a great deal if we look at last season, when 15 of the 20 teams finished within three places of where they were after 10 games.

Aston Villa made the biggest jump, going from 11th at this stage to secure a top-four finish with time to spare.

So Champions League qualification remains well within grasp for Unai Emery's side, who are currently in 10th.

On the other extreme were Tottenham, riding high in sixth after 10 games before plummeting 11 places down the standings to finishing 17th, only securing survival on the final day.

As mentioned earlier, the top two and two of the eventual bottom three were already in their final positions by this point, while Burnley - the third relegated side - were only a place above the drop zone in 17th.

Perhaps Manchester United are in a relegation battle after all...?

'Tinkerman' Alonso's Chelsea side still searching for identity

#922. Who will win ATP Finals in Turin? Alcaraz favourite to land first title

Who will win the season-ending tournament in Italy? Are world No 1 Alexander Zverev and No 2 Carlos Alcaraz on collision course? You can watch the Nitto ATP Finals from November 15-22 in Turin on Sky Sports Tennis

World No 1 Alexander Zverev and second seed Carlos Alcaraz are among the favourites the win the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin - but what do our Sky Sports panel think?

#921. Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

Watch: Cleaning, shirt swaps & video games - the Charles bros at home

Pierce Charles can't help but smile as he waits for Shea to walk into the kitchen.

It's Shea's 23rd birthday and he has a cake to surprise him, something he knows will embarrass his older brother.

Right on cue, he gets the response that he was looking for as Shea has a sheepish smile, and Pierce launches into a rendition of 'Happy Birthday' for the cameras.

In an exclusive interview at their London home, the brothers talk about breaking lamps while playing football as kids, debating who does the chores and the upcoming release of video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

With a cup of tea offered and shoes off at the door, you wouldn't think you were chatting with two international footballers, especially two who are riding the crest of a wave on the pitch.

London traffic aside, they are enjoying life in the hustle and bustle of the city as they live in England's capital for the first time.

"It's better than I thought it was going to be, I didn't think I was going to enjoy it," said Pierce who is spending the season on loan at Queens Park Rangers from Manchester City.

"I actually love it, and living together has been good. There's so much to do in London," added midfielder Shea, who joined Fulham from Southampton in a Â£30m move in August.

Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams

NI win in Georgia after Kvaratskhelia penalty miss

It is the first time the brothers have lived in London, but the third time they have lived together.

Having been born and grown up in Manchester, they came through Manchester City's academy before Pierce joined Sheffield Wednesday aged 16.

Shea stayed at the Etihad and made his Premier League debut under Pep Guardiola in May 2023 before signing for Southampton that summer.

The brothers were reunited at Wednesday when Shea joined on loan for the 2024-25 campaign, but there was some 200 miles between them last year as the midfielder returned to St Mary's.

This summer, after impressive performances for Wednesday and Northern Ireland, Pierce returned to Manchester City in a long-term deal before joining QPR on loan.

Not to be outdone, Shea earned a switch back to the Premier League with Fulham as he became Northern Ireland's first Â£30m footballer.

Both based in west London, that gave them the opportunity to move back in together, reigniting debates over who is better at the Grand Theft Auto games and Fortnite and who cooks the better steak sandwich.

They both want to claim top honours, but Pierce feels he will have the edge if he can get the peppercorn sauce recipe off the chef at QPR.

Older brother Eoin and parents Mary and Kelvin often come to visit, too, and there's more debate over who makes the house presentable, and whether doing the dishwasher actually counts as a chore.

"I think she secretly wants it to be messy, so she can have a little dig at us and do it anyway," jokes Pierce about Mary, who was born in Northern Ireland.

"She enjoys it really, she's not on holiday," Shea laughs.

Quickly realising the danger of getting a telling off on her next visit, Shea adds, "Mum is class. We appreciate mum".

Things quickly get competitive between the brothers over a game of two touch

Before the brothers sit down for a chat, there's time for a kick about in the garden for a game of 'two touch'.

It doesn't take long for their competitive side to shine through, and a best of three quickly becomes best of five then, eventually, a rematch.

Conversation turns to memories of similar games in the family garden as kids and how things used to always take a similarly competitive turn.

"When we used to play Wembley I would have always beaten you two and the loser went in nets," said Shea.

"If you want a fun fact, people might think he is the best player now but Shea was actually the worst out of us when we were younger in the back garden," Pierce was quick to respond.

"It was me, then Eoin and then Shea. To be fair, he's improved massively since."

There's a blame game over a broken clock and lamp, and middle child Shea has to plead his innocence over the latter.

"I broke the clock but I didn't break the lamp. It actually wasn't me, I swear," recalled Shea, still pleading his case before a mischievous "I loved that lamp" almost makes him look guilty.

'No candles?' - Pierce's birthday surprise for Shea

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Fourteen years on from watching the Olympics, Pierce Charles made a late double save to earn QPR a draw at West Ham's London Stadium

The brothers have yet to hit London's tourist spots since moving to the capital, but a trip to Thorpe Park just outside the city is on the cards.

Their first memories of London are from visiting their cousins growing up, and there have been trips to Wembley to see childhood club Manchester City.

But the London 2012 Olympics stand out as an early memory, when the brothers would have been eight and nine years of age.

They remember meeting Team GB heptathlete Katarina Johnson-Thompson and recall racing outside of the London Stadium.

"There were little events on outside the stadium," Shea recalled.

"Like the 50 metres and that sort of stuff. I won my race."

Now the home of West Ham United, both brothers have played at the ground this season, some 14 years on from watching the Olympics at the same venue.

When QPR visited West Ham in October, Pierce was the hero as he saved Jarrod Bowen's last-gasp penalty to deny the Hammers three points.

His man of the match trophy from that game is proudly displayed in their home.

"It looks so much different from what I remember," said Shea on the London Stadium.

"And then we're playing in it 14 years later," added Pierce.

"It's mad, we're getting on a bit aren't we?"

Pierce and Shea Charles both had big moments as Northern Ireland won in Georgia in September

The Charles brothers are just two players in a young and exciting Northern Ireland squad.

Michael O'Neill's side currently top Group B2 in the Nations League after four matches, and they have yet to concede a goal.

The campaign started in Georgia in September and both Shea and Pierce played their part in a famous win.

Pierce saved a penalty from Paris Saint-Germain star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, and also made another big intervention to deny Georges Mikautadze.

Then, nine minutes into additional time, Shea popped up with a late winner to kick-start a window that would see Northern Ireland top their Nations League group after four matches, without conceding a goal.

"I think that's what started the good run," said Pierce.

"You can't win a game like that and fall off."

Highlights: Northern Ireland leave it late to beat Georgia

Now, Northern Ireland will look to finish the job as they host Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday, and finish the campaign in Hungary on 17 November.

"Two wins would be the dream and it would set us up nicely for the next few years," said Pierce.

"The next few games will be tough but we can't wait."

Given they live together and will be in Northern Ireland camp side-by-side - do they get sick of each other?

"It feels like I can't get away from you when we're on camp, but at least it's not shared rooms," said Shea.

"We're just joined at the hip," said Pierce, who added he doesn't get fed up with spending time with his brother.

"We're always together but we're not always together, if you know what I mean."

#919. How Germany's greatest goalscorer is guiding the next generation

Miroslav Klose's FC Nuremberg side sit second in the 2. Bundesliga

It is no surprise Miroslav Klose recognises the value of a true goalscorer.

He is, after all, Germany's all-time leading marksman and until this summer had netted more than any other player in men's World Cup history. Even now, only Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi can top his 16 across four tournaments.

But of the more than 300 goals Klose scored in a career that began in Germany's amateur leagues and spanned Kaiserslautern, Werder Bremen, Bayern Munich and Lazio, he reckons all but two came inside the penalty area.

"Thankfully, we've moved away a little from the idea of the false nine or having a second striker playing around the main striker, with everyone coming towards the ball," explains the FC Nuremberg boss.

"For me, the most important thing is that you need someone who is there to score goals. You need someone in the box because that's where you're closest to the goal. That's why I'm a big believer in practising the final ball, whether it's a cross, a shot or something else.

"That's crucial. How do you create that final ball? When you develop automatisms and players get to know each other better, that's when you see harmony on the pitch.

"It can make things look effortless, but it involves a huge amount of work. A lot of work in training and attention to detail, making sure the players communicate with each other and understand their team-mates' strengths and weaknesses."

That focus on detail stems from Klose's diligence during his playing days. He would study opponents' movement, analyse a goalkeeper's position and shape when facing certain shots - do they make themselves big? Are their hands high or low?

"When goals are scored, the whole team deserves credit," adds the 48-year-old, who was as selfless as he was ruthless. "But you still need someone who has that ability in their feet or in their head to put the ball in the net."

"He's a great role model for me" - Former German forward on Harry Kane

Klose was 36 when he won the World Cup with Germany in 2014 - surpassing Ronaldo's goal record in a 7-1 semi-final thrashing of hosts Brazil.

It was the culmination of a career built on hard work after a series of near-misses - something that may offer solace to Harry Kane and England that a major tournament triumph remains possible.

Born in communist Poland, Klose's father Josef - also a footballer, most notably for Auxerre - moved the family to West Germany when his son was eight.

He was never in a big academy, playing in the lower leagues while training as a carpenter before eventually joining Kaiserslautern.

Klose, like Kane, was in his early 20s by the time he established himself in top-flight football, but just two years after his Bundesliga debut was starting a World Cup final defeat by Brazil.

The striker, 38 when he hung up his goalscoring boots, admires the way Kane has evolved as he has matured, using him as an example to his own young prospects.

"You could always see his quality, and he's worked incredibly hard to get where he is," says Klose of the Ballon d'Or winner.

"He's also a great role model for me, particularly because he has stayed in Germany. I often tell my players that they should look at someone like him as an example.

"Young players can't yet have the instinct and experience he has developed, but that's where it starts - thinking about what you can and can't do as a footballer. You have to keep learning. That's the crucial thing for me.

"If you understand that you train to become better, then in five years' time you'll naturally be a different player. But if you think everything will happen automatically just because 10 people around you tell you that you're a fantastic player, I don't think you'll continue to develop."

Klose's Nuremberg have the youngest average age in the 2. Bundesliga

Klose has a knack for working with young talent, previously coaching Bayern Munich's under-17s. His Nuremberg side are the youngest in the German second tier with an average age of 23.3 years, according to Transfermarkt.

"You need that balance and a certain core of experienced players," he explains. "But we're very brave in that respect. Over the three years I've been here, we've made progress in how we assess young players and in the conversations we have about them.

"How do we rate them? How far along are they? What do they need to work on to take the next step? Is it perhaps more about their physical development? Because from a footballing perspective, we're already producing some really good players."

Klose's coaching journey began with the national team before he joined Bayern, briefly becoming Hansi Flick's assistant, and then took his first managerial role at Rheindorf Altach in Austria.

He joined Nuremberg, historically one of Germany's most successful clubs, in 2024 and steered them to 10th and eighth-placed finishes.

This season they sit second, behind Hertha BSC, and are the league's joint-top scorers, with eyes on a return to the Bundesliga for the first time since 2019.

"When I first arrived, I spoke to the youth coaches about the club's DNA and its coaching philosophy, and what they focus on," adds Klose.

"There was already a lot of common ground. We suggested trying certain things because we wanted to do a little more in particular areas, and they were open to that.

"That's important. We benefit from this because our young players are getting opportunities in the first team, and everyone is paying attention to their development.

"But that journey starts with the youth coaches. I know how important it is to take those steps. We're benefiting from that now because we have access to so many young talents.

"As a coaching team, we're brave enough to give them opportunities when we see that they can compete at this level. That's the first step."

Among the 11 to play the most minutes for Klose's side this season, seven are 22 years old or under, including top scorer Mohamed Ali Zoma, already capped by Italy.

"Of course, everyone gets a lot of praise, as is currently the case with Marc Kornwachs," says Klose of a 17-year-old midfielder also catching the eye.

"But his journey isn't over yet. Now it's about helping him become more consistent and establishing himself, while continuing to develop his game and take further steps forward.

"These players are so talented that we have absolutely no hesitation in giving them opportunities, regardless of the scoreline."

Klose was still playing fifth-tier amateur football aged 20 before becoming the World Cup's all-time top goalscorer in 2014

Klose also understands his managerial career is still young - mirroring the humble nature that earned him fair play awards in Germany and Italy.

"I'm very comfortable with the steps I've taken, even though it involves a huge amount of work," he says about his progress. "You learn something every day.

"I've said that I'm already a much better manager than I was three years ago. That's perfectly normal, and you have to embrace it. I've always been willing and eager to learn, and I've always been a hard worker. That isn't going to change."

So what does a Miroslav Klose team look like?

"Personally, as a player, I always liked having the ball for long periods, and that hasn't changed," he explains.

"When you have the ball, you have a certain level of dominance. I know you also have to be very adaptable in terms of possession, and that's something we are. We constantly show the players different ways of playing out of situations.

"It's great to see how they develop and to be able to support individual players along the way. That's exactly the approach I like to take as a manager."

#915. How promotion, relegation and knockouts work in Nations League

England are closing in on reaching the knockout rounds of the 2026-27 Uefa Nations League

England go into their final two 2026-27 Nations League matches on the brink of qualification for the quarter-finals.

Thomas Tuchel's side sit second after four matches in Group A3, with a point in either of their final two matches in November against Croatia and Spain enough to secure a place in the final eight teams.

November's international break is the final two full rounds of matches, with four rounds already complete.

The eight teams to finish in the top two of the four League A groups will play in the knockout rounds that start in March 2027.

Teams finishing at the top of groups in leagues B and C will earn promotion for the next Nations League cycle, while teams that finish second in a League B or League C group will face either a third-placed or bottom-placed team from the league above them in a promotion/relegation play-off.

The two worst sides to finish bottom of a League A group are automatically relegated. The other bottom sides in League A, third-placed sides in League A and bottom-placed sides in League B are at risk of relegation.

The losers of the play-offs will be relegated.

As the Nations League format is changing for the next cycle, taking place across 2028 and 2029, all League D teams are guaranteed promotion to League C.

Additionally, no teams from League C will be relegated at the end of this cycle.

The new format will consist of three larger leagues, meaning there will not be a League D in the next campaign.

Portugal and Spain are the only sides guaranteed to play in the quarter-finals at present, having both won their opening four matches.

England, who are three points behind Spain in Group A3, are six points clear of third-placed Croatia and with a significantly superior head-to-head record. Unless England were to lose 7-0 or worse to Croatia on Thursday, the Three Lions will be certain of a place in the last eight.

In Group A1, France and Italy sit in the top two spots. Belgium are a point behind Italy in third. Two of those three sides will advance to the quarter-finals.

It is a similar tale in Group A2. Netherlands and Greece are the top two, three points clear of Germany in third. With Serbia bottom on zero points, two of the current top three will advance.

In A4, Denmark are second and three points clear of Wales and Norway. One of the trio will join table-toppers Portugal.

The quarter-finals are played across two legs in March's international break.

The winners of each tie will advance to the semi-finals in June 2027, which are played in a one-off match across Wednesday 9 and Thursday 10 June. The final takes place on Sunday, 13 June.

Wales are in a three-way battle alongside Norway and Denmark to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals

While England's League A campaign has gone well so far, Wales' has been trickier.

In a tough group with Portugal, Denmark and Norway, Wales have picked up three points from four games after beating Norway 2-1 in Cardiff.

With Portugal already qualified for the last eight, Wales will need close to maximum points in their final matches against Norway and Portugal to stand any chance of making the last eight.

A third-place finish would put them in a play-off to avoid relegation in March, while coming last in the group may ensure a drop down to League B.

Scotland are now unable to reach the top spot in Group B1 and are unlikely to make the promotion/relegation play-offs.

In order to finish second, Scotland need to win both of their final two games and hope Slovenia pick up no more than a point from theirs. Alternatively, Scotland can pick up four points and finish second, providing Slovenia lose their final two matches.

Northern Ireland have had a successful international break with two wins, two draws and no goals conceded in their four matches in Group B2.

They sit top of the group by a point, with their remaining matches against bottom side Ukraine and second-place Hungary.

Should they beat Ukraine and Hungary fail to beat Georgia in November's first round of fixtures, they will guarantee top spot and promotion. A win for them and Hungary doing the same would mean the two sides face off in a promotion-decider in the final round of games.

The Republic of Ireland are third in Group B3 following five points from their first four matches.

Their remaining two fixtures are against the top two teams Austria and Kosovo. Wins in both would guarantee a top-two finish and would also put them in a strong position to win the group, depending on goal difference and the result of Austria's meeting with Israel.

Spain are the current holders of the European Championship, beating England in the 2024 final

Once the Nations League campaign is concluded, all 54 competing nations will be ranked based on their performance in this edition of the competition.

That ranking will have a direct impact on qualification for the 2028 European Championships, being held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

The Nations League ranking will also determine the seeding of nations for Euro 2028 qualification.

Regular qualifying will take place between March and November 2027, with play-offs for the remaining spots in the tournament to take place in March 2028.

As there are four co-hosts and none of them have been granted immediate qualification, the number of how many qualify will effectively determine how many play-off spots will be up for grabs.

Uefa have said that up to two places will be given to the best-ranked co-hosts that fail to qualify for the tournament via its primary qualification route.

Scenarios have already been designed for occurrences where either two, one or zero co-hosts are given entry spots.

Depending on which play-off format is required, either eight or 12 teams will enter.

A total of 24 teams will enter the European Championships, 20 of them will consist of the winners of the 12 qualifying groups and the eight best runners-up from those group.

The remaining runners-up will enter the play-offs, alongside the Nations League group winners from League A, League B and League C that failed to finish in the top two of their Euro 2028 qualifying group.

If extra teams are required, the best-ranked League D group winner will enter the play-offs.

Any additional play-off spots that become available after that will filter down to the next-highest ranked Nations League finishers until the play-off spots are filled.

#914. English Soccer Star Jude Bellingham Reveals He Can’t Drive or Cook

Jude Bellingham, star of England’s men’s soccer team and Real Madrid, admitted his skills are limited to the pitch, and that he hasn’t yet learned how to drive or cook.

Jude Bellingham may be one of the greatest footballers of his generation.

But as it turns out, Team England’s star midfielder’s basic everyday skills—or lack thereof—help level the playing field, bringing him closer to us mere mortals.

“There’s loads of things I don’t know how to do,” Bellingham told British Vogue in an interview published Nov. 10. “I can’t cook, I can’t drive. I’m good at what I do, but everything else? Not that great. I rely on my friends, my family to help me do stuff—chef, cleaner, mum, whoever else. That’s where I’m at.”

In fact, he’s been so busy keeping his eye on the literal ball—and doing a really good job at it—he may have lost track of life’s other skills.

“I work hard every day and all day, and then when I get home,” the 23-year-old said, “I’ve probably neglected learning how to do some of the more basic things.”

In his defense, not only is learning those life skills par for the course for many early twenty-somethings, but Bellingham’s daytime job also takes up a lot of his time.

“I feel mature in a football context because I’ve played nearly 400 games,” he reflected. “But in a life context I don’t feel that mature now, to be honest.”

But, as he noted, “There’ll be a time and a place for that, I’m sure.”

In the meantime, he’s focused on his skills on the pitch, where Bellingham’s natural talents already having brough him to the World Cup twice, in 2022 and 2026. And in their most recent outing, England finished third—the country’s best result since 1966.

“The World Cup, for me, was probably the best experience I’ve had in my life, full stop,” the Real Madrid player said. “While I was in it, I really made the conscious decision to enjoy this.”

After all, “It doesn’t come around very often,” he added. “It’s rare.”

And while Bellingham’s World Cup performance won him fans around the world—as did his endearing bromance with former Borussia Dortmund teammate and Norway’s star Erling Haaland—nowhere was more grateful for his performance than England.

As he noted, “I’ve seen a lot of people say, ‘I don’t think I’ve ever had a night when I was so happy and so proud to be English.’”

For a look back at the many celebrities who tuned in live to see Bellingham’s athletic prowess shine on the pitch, read on.

#913. England's Blues brothers - how the Bellinghams helped save Birmingham

Jude Bellingham shared an old photo of him and brother Jobe after England's squad announcement last week

It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

While Jude, 23, is establishing himself as a footballing great at European greats Real Madrid following a spell at Borussia Dortmund, Jobe, 21, is continuing his football education at his brother's former club in Germany after two seasons with Sunderland.

The Stourbridge-born midfielders have moved on with their careers.

Their memories, however, live on at St Andrew's, such was the impact the boyhood Birmingham fans made in the Championship.

On match days supporters stop and pose for photographs in front of Jude's mural outside the ground. Fans still turn up to matches wearing Bellingham shirts.

"They both had a real connection with fans," Craig Courtney, from the Tilton Talk fan podcast, told BBC Sport. "Fans loved the fact they both cared.

"They wore their hearts on their sleeves and helped Birmingham when we were fighting relegation. Even now, Jude and Jobe remember where it all started for them."

The brothers played 70 league and cup games between them for Birmingham after graduating from the academy.

They have never appeared together in a senior match, however, as Jude - who joined Birmingham aged eight - had left by the time Jobe broke into the first team in 2022.

The Bellinghams will become the first brothers to play for England for 19 years if Jobe wins his first cap and appears alongside Jude, a veteran of 60 appearances, in the Nations League game with Croatia at Wembley.

"It will be an incredibly proud moment for Birmingham City if that happens," said Courtney.

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

Listen: How Jude Bellingham became a global brand

Birmingham supporters have had little to cheer about recently.

It is 15 years since they last appeared in the Premier League, while the 2011 League Cup winners even dipped down to League One recently.

While fierce rivals Aston Villa were playing - and beating - Bayern Munich and Bologna in the Champions League two years ago, Birmingham were losing at Shrewsbury and drawing with Northampton Town.

After 15 games Birmingham sit top of the Championship and there are plans for a new 62,000-capacity stadium in time for 2030-31.

"As a club, we've been right down in the doldrums," added Courtney. "Now we're top of the table and having a new stadium built.

"There is an argument that none of this would have been possible without the fees received for Jude and Jobe."

A mural tribute to Jude Bellingham outside St Andrew's

Jude is the youngest player in Birmingham's history after making his debut aged 16 years and 38 days in 2019.

Clubs across Europe were pursuing him when he signed his first professional contact in 2020 after turning 17 - a deal both he and Birmingham knew would never be fulfilled.

His actions, however, ensured Birmingham would receive a significant transfer fee when he left, and soon afterwards he joined Dortmund for an initial fee of Â£20m during the Covid-19 pandemic.

When he joined Real in 2023, Birmingham received a reported sell-on fee of at least Â£10m., external

"We cannot possibly imagine, without Jude's decision [to sign a contract], where we would be as a club in a pandemic like this," then Birmingham chief executive Xuandong Ren told BBC WM after Jude joined Dortmund.

"He could easily have just looked after himself and not the club, but he chose the best possible way to look after the club."

Jobe became the second youngest player to play for Birmingham when he made his debut in January 2022 aged 16 years and 107 days.

"This was a lad, regardless of who his brother was or what he was achieving, who would do anything to write his own success story," former Birmingham striker Troy Deeney, who played in the game when Jobe made his debut, told the Sun., external

"Everything he has achieved on the pitch, too, has come with an instant comparison to his older brother.

"He never got that one moment to enjoy something without someone, somewhere saying: 'Yeah, but what about Jude?'

"That only added to how strong he was mentally, and anyone who suggests he is where he is because of his last name is talking rubbish."

Deeney added: "What impressed me more than anything he had done on the pitch was his attitude - a hell-bent determination to get to the top and the common sense to take all the right steps along the way."

Jobe played 26 games before Sunderland paid Â£3m for him in 2023, with Birmingham receiving a reported Â£4m sell-on fee when he moved to Dortmund two years later.

Although significantly less than the fees generated by his brother, it was nevertheless welcome revenue.

Jobe Bellingham was given his Birmingham City debut by manager Lee Bowyer in January 2022

Both Jude and Jobe have returned to St Andrew's since their transfers.

Jobe captained England Under-21s to a 2-0 win against the Republic of Ireland at his old ground last November.

Before that match U21s boss Lee Carsley, who managed Jude when he was England interim manager in 2024, praised the brothers for their work ethic and determination to be the best.

Carsley said: "I know how much they love the Blues still and how important the club is to them."

Jude, tipped to be a future England captain, was at St Andrew's in July watching his former club in a pre-season friendly against Barcelona. He even wore a Birmingham shirt while watching from the stands.

Jude wore a Birmingham City shirt when he returned to St Andrew's

When Jude joined Dortmund in 2020 Birmingham retired the 17-year-old's number 22 shirt after 44 appearances.

"That was a gesture of thanks for what Jude had done," said Courtney.

"It might be wishful thinking, but I really believe Jude has unfinished business at Birmingham. I can see a scenario before he retires where he gets an opportunity to wear the number 22 again."

Should the Bellingham brothers play together against Croatia, they will become the first siblings to appear for England since Gary and Phil Neville against Spain in a friendly at Old Trafford in 2007.

It will be an immensely proud moment for their parents, Mark and Denise.

"We've played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life," Jude, a Champions League and La Liga winner with Real Madrid, wrote on social media, external in 2024.

"That would mean more than any of the trophies. Nothing would even get close to that... nothing."

BBC reporter John Watson has been finding out why Bellingham is proving so popular with football fans across the world

#912. From W-M to the No 10, shirt numbers tell a story of football’s tactical evolution

In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, as well as the attributes a player was supposed to demonstrate

Ultimate 1-50: check out our complete list of players

Numbers have a fascination. The No 10 is revered almost everywhere, but perhaps most especially in Argentina, where it denotes the playmaker, the enganche, the quasi-mythical figure who links the front and back of the team. Liverpool and Manchester United have reasons to celebrate their No 7. Ajax retired No 14 for Johan Cruyff, Milan their No 3 and No 6 for Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi respectively and Birmingham their 22 for Jude Bellingham as gestures of respect for their abilities. Other numbers have been retired to mark premature deaths: the No 20 at Liverpool for Diogo Jota, the No 23 at Manchester City for Marc-Vivien Foé, the 21 at Espanyol for Daniel Jarque.

But numbers are not just about individuals. In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, and the expectations of particular numbers in particular cultures, as well as the attributes a player in that shirt was supposed to demonstrate, themselves tell a story of tactical evolution.

The earliest evidence of teams wearing numbered shirts seems to be in a game between the Australian sides Sydney Leichhardt and HSM Powerful in 1911. The University of Chicago’s American football team wore squad numbers in 1913. There were experiments with numbers on sleeves in baseball from 1916. There were isolated efforts with numbered shirts in the American Soccer League, which began in 1923, and, especially, in the USA’s Challenge Cup. Various touring sides began to experiment with numbered shirts through the 1920s and, in August 1928, on the opening day of the English league season, two games featured numbers. Chelsea’s outfielders wore 2-11 in their Second Division game against Swansea, while Sheffield Wednesday wore 1-11 and Arsenal 12-22 in a First Division clash at Hillsborough.

Similarly, 1-22 numbering was used in the 1933 FA Cup final, in part because Everton and Manchester City were forced to wear change kits due to a colour clash, although the presence of the touring West Indies cricket side, who were not expected to be familiar with the individual players, was also cited. It wasn’t until June 1939, though, that the Football League took a vote to introduce squad numbers. It passed 24-20, and it was decided both teams should wear 1-11, but in strict order, as though the formation had been laid out on a page with the goalkeeper at the top.

This was complicated by the fact that, although almost every team by that stage had responded to the 1925 change in the offside law by adopting the W-M formation (a 3-2-2-3), there was still a belief that the “right” way to play was a 2-3-5. Thus the goalkeeper wore No 1, the right-back No 2, the left-back No 3, the right-half No 4, the centre-half No 5 and so on up to the centre-forward in No 9, the inside-left in No 10 and the left-winger in No 11. In practice, though, the centre-half (5), played between the full-backs (2 and 3) while the inside-forwards (8 and 10) played deeper than the wingers and centre-forward (7, 9 and 11).

Numbers rapidly became sacrosanct. When Hungary came to Wembley in 1953 and became the first foreign side to beat England at the national stadium, they provoked consternation because they were “incorrectly” numbered. The centre-back Mihaly Lantos wore No 4. The midfield creator Jozsef Bozsik wore No 5. Most bafflingly of all, Nandor Hidegkuti, the No 9, didn’t play as a centre-forward but created from midfield. What was Harry Johnston, England’s hapless centre-half, to do? Convention said he, the No 5, should pick up the No 9, but if he did that he left a huge hole in the back line. And if he did not, Hidegkuti was free to pick England apart.

The introspection provoked by that defeat led within a decade or so to a number of leading English teams adopting a back four, usually by withdrawing the left-half (the No 6) into the defensive line. As Alf Ramsey’s 1966 World Cup winners showed the value of packing midfield, so the wingers dropped back, leaving a 4-4-2 that lined up: 1; 2, 5, 6, 3; 7, 4, 8, 11; 9, 10. Within that, the No 4 would usually be the more defensive of the two central midfielders, while the No 10 retained some of the qualities of the inside-left, which is to say he tended to be the smaller, more creative forward alongside a big, physical No 9.

Other countries, though, followed a different path. In Argentina, for instance, there had been no sudden shift to W-M in the late 1920s but, at River Plate in the late 1930s, the right-half Norberto Yácono, nicknamed “the Stamp” for his tight marking, would pick up the opposing creator. As other teams followed the principle, the No 4 became a de facto third back, but operating on the right. No 4 remains the standard number for an Argentinian right-back, as exemplified by Javier Zanetti, for whom Inter retired the shirt. When Argentina switched to a back four after the humiliation of the 6-1 defeat to Czechoslovakia at the 1958 World Cup, the left-half fell into the back line, so a standard Argentinian back four would read: 4, 2, 6, 3. The No 5 remained as the caudillo in midfield, almost as venerated as the No 10 in the form of Antonio Rattín, Américo Gallego and Javier Mascherano.

In Brazil, though, there had been no widespread conversion of the right-half into a right-back, and so when the back four was adopted, the wing-halves simply dropped either side of the full-backs, leaving a standard back four as: 4, 2, 3, 6. The great right-back Carlos Alberto, for instance, wore No 4 at the 1970 World Cup, while the left-back Roberto Carlos tended to wear No 6. When, at Flamengo in the 1940s, Flávio Costa tipped the midfield square of Dori Kürschner’s W-M to create his diagonal, a major step towards 4-2-4, the No 5 became the more defensive central midfielder – leading to players such as Clodoaldo, Mauro Silva and Casemiro wearing the shirt for the national team – while the inside-left, the No 10, became the most creative midfielder.

In other countries, other conventions emerged. It was in the Netherlands and West Germany that the standard delineations of the expectations on midfielders in a 4-3-3 emerged. The No 6 would be the deep-lying player, the No 10 would be the creator, and the No 8 would be a box-to-box player shuttling between them. Or in France, where a five-man bench from which a manger could use two substitutes was adopted in 1976, it became standard for the reserve goalkeeper to wear No 16. Many goalkeepers in the Francophone world gained their first experience wearing No 16 and so favoured it when squad numbers were introduced: that’s why Fabian Barthez wore No 16 at the 1998 World Cup and Cameroon’s Thomas N’Kono wore it in 1990.

Numbers now are often a matter of personal choice and of brand-building. In a squad system, players can take on a familiar number and hope to embody its spirit, or try to make a more obscure number their own, as Johan Cruyff did with the No 14 more than half a century ago.

Numbers have a past, and they tell a story. Nobody on the Football League committee that narrowly voted to mandate squad numbers in 1939 would have considered the possibility, but in numbers are written the deep history of a country’s tactical development.

#911. Kane's top 10 England moments - which was your favourite?

"Amazing" Kane targets 100 international goals

Harry Kane will become England's most capped player against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday.

The 33-year-old Ballon d'Or winner has scored a record 91 goals in 125, soon to be 126, matches for his country.

We look at 10 of his most iconic moments in an England jersey - not counting the moment he almost lost his voice in a BBC interview after the summer's World Cup quarter-final win over Mexico.

England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender

Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record

Harry Kane scored with just his third touch in international football

Kane started his England career with a goal after just 79 seconds and three touches - in a 4-0 Euro 2016 qualifying win over Lithuania in March 2015.

Then 21 and in his first season as a Tottenham regular, he came on in the 70th minute before heading in Raheem Sterling's cross at Wembley.

The BBC match report called him "the man with the Midas touch in front of goal this season".

Harry Kane was England captain at his second major tournament, the 2018 World Cup

Kane has scored 21 major tournament goals for England, which is a record.

His first two - having failed to bag at Euro 2016 - came against Tunisia at the 2018 World Cup as captain.

He netted the opener after John Stones' header was saved and nodded in a stoppage-time winner to give England a 2-1 win in Volgograd, Russia.

Harry Kane has scored four goals against Panama at World Cups

Kane's first England hat-trick came in their next game, a 6-1 win over Panama in the World Cup in Nizhny Novgorod.

He scored two penalties and then deflected in Ruben Loftus-Cheek's shot for probably one of his easiest career hat-tricks.

Harry Kane finished two goals ahead of anyone else at the 2018 World Cup

That summer Kane became the second Englishman to win a World Cup Golden Boot, after Gary Lineker, with six goals.

The sixth was his penalty to give England a 1-0 lead over Colombia in the last 16.

Colombia equalised but Kane also scored in the shootout to help the Three Lions through.

Harry Kane made England's win over Germany safe at the Covid-delayed Euro 2020

Kane was again involved in the goals as England beat Germany in a knockout game for the first time in 55 years, to reach the Euro 2020 quarter-finals in 2021.

The striker nodded in from Jack Grealish's cross with four minutes remaining to seal a 2-0 win at Wembley.

Harry Kane was denied by former Leicester team-mate Kasper Schmeichel but netted the rebound at Euro 2020

One of the biggest goals of Kane's career was the extra-time winner over Denmark to take them into the Euro 2020 final.

His penalty was saved by Denmark's Kasper Schmeichel but the rebound came back to him to score in a 2-1 Wembley win.

That was England's first men's major tournament final since the 1966 World Cup.

Harry Kane overtook Wayne Rooney's England scoring record at the age of 29

Kane became England's all-time record goalscorer with his 54th goal in March 2023, taking him past Wayne Rooney, with their first away win against Italy since 1964.

He scored a first-half penalty as the Three Lions started their Euro 2024 qualifying campaign with a 2-1 win in Naples.

The striker has since extended that record by another 37 goals.

Harry Kane was the joint top scorer at Euro 2024 with three goals

England fell behind early on in their Euro 2024 semi-final match against the Netherlands in Dortmund.

But then Kane equalised from the spot in the first half - before Ollie Watkins' last-minute winner to take them to the final.

It was his second European Championship semi-final goal in two attempts

Harry Kane was awarded a golden cap before his 100th cap

Kane was awarded a golden cap and wore golden boots to mark his 100th England appearance in a Nations League match against Finland in 2024.

And he marked the occasion with both goals in a 2-0 win at Wembley, smashing an effort in off the underside of the bar and then curling in a second.

Kane scores late winner as England overcome DR Congo to reach last 16

England's 2026 World Cup campaign almost ended with a last-32 embarrassment against DR Congo.

But Kane stepped up to save them with two goals in the final 15 minutes.

He headed in the equaliser before smashing in a brilliant winner on the turn with four minutes remaining.

In the next round he netted against Mexico and made headlines with a squeaky-voiced post-match interview in the Azteca altitude...

'I'm speechless' - Kane reacts to England's victory over Mexico

#910. Ghana kick-start Afcon 2027 bid despite Ayew penalty miss

Jordan Ayew joined Championship side Sheffield United in September after spending two seasons with Leicester City

Ghana belatedly kick-started their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifying campaign with a 2-0 home win over Somalia.

The Black Stars had lost their opening two Group C matches against Ivory Coast and The Gambia, leading to the departure of coach Carlos Queiroz by mutual consent.

Ghana women's coach Kim Bjorkegren was placed in interim charge for this month's double-header against the Ocean Stars, with the West Africans in danger of missing a second successive edition of the Afcon finals.

The hosts were given a chance to take an early lead in Sekondi-Takoradi after Alidu Seidu was pulled down in the box, but Jordan Ayew's 14th-minute penalty was saved by Somalia goalkeeper Ibrahim Hussein.

Ghana did go ahead in first-half stoppage time when Mohammed Salisu headed Mohammed Kudus's deep corner back across goal and Jonas Adjetey nodded in from six yards out.

Felix Afena-Gyan doubled the Black Stars' advantage just after the hour mark when his shot from inside the box squirmed under Hussein and over the line.

The four-time continental champions remain six points behind group leaders Ivory Coast, who extended their 100% record by beating The Gambia 2-1 in Bouake.

Brighton midfielder Malick Yalcouye tucked in from seven yards out and Elye Wahi slotted home to double the Elephants' lead before Musa Barrow pulled one back for the visitors before the break.

Elsewhere on Thursday, there were wins for Cameroon, DR Congo and Senegal, who all remain on track to qualify for next year's tournament in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

The third round of qualifying fixtures continues on Friday with Egypt, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa in action among 12 fixtures.

Nicolas Jackson has 11 goals in 17 appearances for club and country this season

Nicolas Jackson set Senegal on their way to a 4-1 home win over Sudan in Group J, with Aston Villa team-mate Ibrahim Mbaye also on the scoresheet for Patrick Vieira's men in Dakar.

The Teranga Lions lead the standings on seven points, three ahead of Mozambique, who host Ethiopia on Friday.

Cameroon also remained unbeaten and moved on to seven points in Group G with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Namibia in Douala.

Meanwhile, Newcastle United striker Yoane Wissa opened the scoring as DR Congo continued their perfect start with a 3-1 triumph over Sierra Leone in Kinshasa.

The Leopards are on nine points at the top of Group E, five points ahead of Zimbabwe and Equatorial Guinea after those two sides drew 0-0.

Nigeria were handed a boost after Group L leaders Guinea-Bissau could only manage a 1-1 draw in their away tie against Madagascar in neutral Morocco.

The Super Eagles trail Guinea-Bissau by four points ahead of their home game against Tanzania on Friday (16:00 GMT).

Tanzania are assured of a place at Afcon 2027 as tournament co-hosts, with the other three sides battling for one qualification spot.

And Benin bolstered their bid to reach back-to-back finals with a 4-1 win over Central African Republic.

Gernot Rohr's Cheetahs lead Group F by three points from Burkina Faso, who entertain Mauritania on Friday.

In Group D, another section with just one spot available, Guinea moved level on points with table-toppers South Africa after seeing off Eritrea 2-1 in Conakry.

Benin 4-1 Central African Republic (Group F)
